opus-5.5.text:
I think the core reason is that the general-purpose models are getting extremely capable, but capability in the abstract isn't the same as being reliably useful inside a specific kind of work. When you go deep on a category, say software engineering, or legal work, or financial analysis, you start to see that the last mile is where most of the value actually lives. It's the specific workflows, the tools people use, the ways they judge whether something is good or not, the failure modes that matter in that domain. A frontier lab building a horizontal model is optimizing for breadth, and that's the right call for them, but it means there's a lot of room for companies that obsess over one domain and close that gap.

There's also a technical argument. A lot of what made these models dramatically better recently is reinforcement learning on top of pretraining, and RL works best when you have a clear notion of what good looks like, a reward signal you can trust. If you're focused on a particular category of work, you can build much better environments, evaluations, and feedback loops for that category than a general lab can for every category at once. So you get compounding advantages: you understand the users better, you collect better data on what success means, you train against it, the product gets better, and more people use it.

And then there's the product side. Deep agents that actually do work, not just answer questions, need to be woven into how people operate day to day. That requires a lot of opinionated design decisions that only make sense if you really know the domain. So my expectation is that we'll see a layer of companies that pair strong research with deep domain focus, and those are the ones that'll end up delivering agents people genuinely trust to do meaningful work on their behalf.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about it is that the general-purpose models are going to keep getting better, and I don't think that's in question. But there's a big gap between a model that's really smart in a general sense and a system that actually does a specific job reliably. If you think about what it takes to be good at, say, software engineering or legal work or scientific research, it's not just raw intelligence. It's a huge amount of context, it's knowing the tools, it's knowing what good looks like in that domain, and it's getting feedback from the environment over a long horizon.

That last part is really the key for me. The way we got models that are genuinely capable at things like math and code was by building environments where the model can act, get a signal about whether it did the right thing, and improve from that. Reinforcement learning works when you have that loop. And building that loop for a particular category of work is hard. You need the right data, you need verifiable outcomes, you need to understand the workflow deeply enough to design the task well. That's not something a general lab is going to do for every single vertical. There are just too many of them.

So I think what you'll see is companies that pick a domain where there's real economic value, go very deep on it, and essentially build the training ground for that domain. They'll own the environment, the evaluation, the feedback signal. And over time the model they produce for that category will be meaningfully better than a general model, not because the base intelligence is higher but because it's been shaped by thousands of iterations of doing the actual work. That's a durable advantage, and it's also just a much more tractable way to get to something that's reliable enough that people trust it with real work.

r002.rationale: It says general models need domain-specific shaping through repeated work and feedback to perform specialized jobs reliably.

r003.rationale: It predicts companies will focus deeply on domains with real economic value and build training grounds for those categories of work.

astra-6.text:
I think it comes down to the difference between having a very capable model and actually getting a job done. A model can be useful across a huge range of tasks, but doing a particular job reliably requires context: what tools people use, what information matters, what a good outcome looks like, and how you check whether you got there.

If you focus deeply on one category of work, you can build that whole loop. You can put the system into the workflow, see where it fails, and use that feedback to make it better. And some of the most valuable feedback is going to come from actually doing the work, rather than from a generic benchmark.

So I expect companies to emerge around that. Their advantage will be understanding a particular job well enough to turn the underlying model capability into something a customer can reliably delegate to.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the reason is that a lot of the difficulty is going to be in figuring out what good performance actually means in a particular job. It’s one thing to have a model that can answer questions about almost anything. It’s another to have a system that can reliably do a piece of work, know when it’s made a mistake, and improve from the feedback it gets.

If you focus deeply on one category of work, you can build the environment around that: the tools, the data, the evaluations, and the feedback loop with the people who actually do the job. That gives you a way to turn a very general capability into something people can trust and pay for.

So I’d expect companies to emerge around those loops. Their advantage won’t necessarily be that they have the best model at everything. It’ll be that they understand a particular kind of work well enough to make the whole system perform exceptionally well at it.
